The shell landed close enough to shower them with dirt and pine needles. Leo flattened himself against the forest floor, the vibrations rattling his teeth. He risked a glance at Pierre, who was already on his feet, brushing off his jacket as though it were merely dust from a country lane. The boy had nerves of solid steel.

"Come on, they will have heard that for certain!" Pierre hissed, yanking Leo up by the collar of his worn coat. "This way! My uncle has a cellar. It is not much, but it is better than a grave."

Leo stumbled after him, his heart hammering against his ribs. They had been running for what felt like days, ever since the ambush on the road to Amiens. They were the only two from their little band of saboteurs to get away clean. "Your uncle won't mind a stray American, will he?" Leo panted.

Pierre shot him a grin over his shoulder. "My uncle will be happy for any news of the outside world that does not come from a German radio!" he said. "He hates them more than he hates sour wine. And that is saying something!"

They burst from the woods into a small, sleeping village. The street was empty, the windows shuttered tight. A dog barked somewhere, a frantic, lonely sound that was quickly silenced. Pierre led them to a squat stone house behind a bakery and rapped on the cellar door in a peculiar rhythm. It creaked open a moment later and a thick arm pulled them inside into the damp, musty blackness.

The door scraped shut, and a match flared. A huge man with a magnificent, drooping mustache and weary eyes stared at them. He looked from Pierre to Leo, his gaze lingering on Leo’s unfamiliar face.

"So," the man rumbled, his voice a low gravel. "The little fox returns. And he brings a friend. An Englishman?"

"American, Uncle Henri," Pierre said quickly. "He is with us. We were separated from our unit."

Henri’s eyes narrowed. He looked at Leo’s boots, his trousers, the exhaustion on his face. "Separated," he repeated, the word full of suspicion. "Or you are a deserter. Or worse. We have had enough trouble here. The Kommandant has promised to shoot ten men for every act of sabotage. Your little fireworks show last night will cost us dearly."

"We fight for France!" Leo snapped, his patience worn thin. "We risk our lives while you hide in a cellar and worry about the Kommandant!"

Henri took a step forward, his big hands curling into fists. "You know nothing, boy! You come here with your guns and your bombs and then you run away, leaving us to face the music. It is our sons and fathers who will stand against the wall, not you!"

"Enough!" Pierre cried, stepping between them. His voice, usually so light, had taken on a sharp, commanding edge. "Listen to me, Uncle! Have you become a coward? Do you think we do this for fun? We have information, vital information, about a troop train coming through tomorrow. It is full of munitions for the front. We were on our way to deliver the message when we were attacked. Is that the act of a deserter? Is that bringing trouble? Or is it bringing a chance, a real chance, to strike a blow?"

He jabbed a finger at Leo. "And him? He crossed an ocean to fight for a country that is not his own. He has fought harder than any man I know. You will show him respect, or you have forgotten what the word means! Now, will you help us, or will you sit here in the dark until the Germans knock on your door to take you away too?"

Henri stared at his nephew, his anger slowly draining away, replaced by a deep, profound weariness. A slow smile touched his lips, but it did not reach his eyes. "He has your mother's fire, this one," he murmured to the air. "Always so sure, so full of righteous anger." He sighed and sank onto a wooden crate. "A troop train, you say? With munitions?"

"Yes," Leo said, his voice quieter now. "Headed for the Ardennes. We have the schedule."

The big baker rubbed his face with his hands. "It is bad, you know," he said in a low tone. "Very bad. We hear whispers. They say Paris is surrounded. They say the fight is almost over. Every day, more gray uniforms in the streets, more rules, less food. We feel the hope draining away like wine from a cracked bottle." He looked up, his eyes bleak. "But a troop train. Yes. That would be something. That would be a good noise to hear."

He stood up, his shoulders seeming a little less slumped. "You cannot stay here. They will search the village house by house. But I know a place. An old quarry. You will be safe there. I will bring you food. And I will get your message to the right people. We are not all cowards, you see. Just tired. Very, very tired."

"Thank you," Leo said simply.

Henri nodded, a flicker of the old strength returning to his face. "Do not thank me. Just make it count, boys. Make the noise loud enough for all of us to hear." He turned and unbarred the door, peering into the pre-dawn gloom. "Go now. And God be with you."

In a small clearing, a field kitchen had been set up. A large black pot steamed over a low fire, and a cook with a magnificent mustache was slicing a long loaf of dark bread. The corporal said a few words to the cook, who grunted and cut two thick slices, topping each with a wedge of yellow cheese. He handed them to the boys without a word, his eyes as tired as the lieutenant's.

"Eat," the corporal said. "It is not much, but it is all we have."

Dave took a bite. The bread was coarse and the cheese was strong, but he had never tasted anything so good in his life. He was so hungry his stomach ached. He and Freddy ate in silence, leaning against the trunk of a great oak tree. The nearness of the fighting, the constant, dull thunder of artillery, seemed a world away in the peaceful quiet of the woods.

"That lieutenant was a good sort," Freddy said after a moment, his mouth full. "He believed us."

"We were lucky," Dave replied, swallowing. "If you hadn't started spouting off like a general, they would have shot us for sure. Where did you learn to talk like that?"

Freddy almost smiled. "My father. He's a diplomat. He says you can get anything you want if you sound like you are supposed to have it. He says most people are too tired to argue with authority."

"Your father sounds like a smart man," Dave said. "These men here, they're not just tired. They're beaten. You can see it in their eyes." He thought of the corporal's rifle, trailing on the ground as though it weighed a ton. "The corporal said there are no British or French here. Only Belgians. What chance do they have?"

Freddy did not answer. He stared into the trees, his young face grim. The food had restored some of his strength, but not his spirits. The truth was a heavy stone in both their stomachs. They had escaped one trap only to land in the middle of a much larger one, a trap that was closing around an entire country.

When they had finished, the corporal led them back through the woods to the winding dirt road. A soldier with a motorcycle and a sidecar was waiting for them, the engine sputtering impatiently. He wore goggles pushed up on his forehead and his face was grimed with oil and dust.

"G.H.Q.?" the rider asked the corporal, his voice a hoarse shout over the noise of the engine.

The corporal nodded. "And be quick about it! This is important!"

"Everything is important today," the rider grunted. He jerked his head at the sidecar. "Get in, one of you. The other on the back. And hold on tight. I do not stop for bumps in the road."

Freddy squeezed into the narrow sidecar, and Dave swung a leg over the seat behind the driver. The corporal gave them a tired wave. "Good luck, my little ones," he called. "Perhaps you will bring us some."

The motorcycle shot forward with a lurch, throwing Dave hard against the driver's back. He grabbed hold of the man's belt and hung on for dear life. They roared down the dirt road and onto a paved highway littered with the debris of war. Overturned farm carts, abandoned cars, and the dark shapes of dead horses lay strewn across the pavement. In the fields on either side, shell craters gaped at the sky like open mouths. The air was thick with the smell of smoke and something else, something sweet and sickening that Dave did not want to identify.

They were heading west, away from the advancing thunder of the front. But the war was not just in front of them. It was above them. The sky was filled with the drone of German planes. They flew in lazy circles, unopposed, like vultures waiting for the kill. Twice, a fighter plane swooped low over the road, and the driver swerved violently, heading for the cover of a line of trees. The rattle of machine gun fire chased them, kicking up spurts of dirt and stone from the roadside. But the pilot was either a bad shot or simply playing with them, and the bullets went wide.

"They own the sky!" the driver yelled back at Dave over his shoulder. "Where is the R.A.F.? Where are the French planes? Do they not know we are dying down here?"

Dave had no answer. He could only press his face against the driver's rough tunic and pray. He felt a new kind of fear, a helpless fear that was worse than being in a dogfight. In a cockpit, he had a stick and a throttle and guns. He could fight back. Down here, he was just a target, a bug on a road waiting to be squashed.

After what seemed like an eternity, they turned off the main highway and raced through the empty streets of a small town. Shutters were drawn tight on all the windows, and not a soul was in sight. It was a ghost town, listening in terror to the approaching storm. On the far side of town, they came to a large chateau surrounded by a high stone wall. Military vehicles were parked haphazardly on the manicured lawns, and staff officers hurried in and out of the main entrance. This was clearly Belgian General Headquarters.

Their driver skidded to a stop at the main gate, which was guarded by two sentries. He exchanged a few hurried words with them, pointing back at Dave and Freddy. A young officer was summoned. He had a clean uniform and a harried expression. He listened to the driver's report, his eyes widening slightly as he looked at the two boys.

"An escape from Germany? With information from a staff map?" he said in crisp, precise French. He looked them up and down, taking in their torn clothes and dirt-smeared faces. "It sounds incredible. But everything is incredible these days. Come with me."

He led them inside the chateau. The interior was a scene of organized chaos. Men shouted into telephones, runners darted back and forth with messages, and staff officers were clustered in anxious groups around maps spread on ornate tables. The air buzzed with tension and despair. Dave felt a sinking feeling in his gut. This did not look like the headquarters of an army that was winning. It looked like the headquarters of an army that was disintegrating.

They were taken to a small, wood paneled office on the second floor. A portly general with a magnificent white mustache and weary, pouchy eyes sat behind a massive desk. He looked up as they entered, and his gaze was sharp and intelligent despite his obvious exhaustion.

"What is this, Captain?" the general asked, his voice gravelly. "I have no time for children's games."

The young captain snapped to attention. "General, these boys claim to have escaped from Germany. They are an American and an Englishman. They say they have seen a German strategic map at a command post near Aachen."

The general's eyes narrowed. He gestured for the captain to leave, then fixed his gaze on Freddy. "You are the Englishman? You speak French?"

"Yes, sir," Freddy said, standing as straight as he could.

"Then talk," the general commanded. "And do not waste my time. Tell me everything."

Freddy began to speak. He told the story quickly and clearly, just as he had for the lieutenant in the woods. He described their capture, their imprisonment in the German headquarters, the map on the wall with its pins and flags, and their escape in the stolen Fieseler Storch. The general listened without interrupting, his fingers steepled under his chin. When Freddy mentioned the concentration of German armor marked on the map, poised to strike through the Ardennes forest, the general's eyes flickered.

When Freddy had finished, the general turned to Dave. "And you, the American. You saw this map as well?"

"Yes, sir," Dave said. "It was just as he described. They had arrows drawn right through the Ardennes. It looked like nobody was there to stop them. They called it 'Sichelschnitt'. The sickle cut."

The general's face went pale under his tan. He leaned forward, his eyes boring into Dave. "They called it that? 'Sichelschnitt'?"

"Yes, sir," Dave confirmed.

The general sank back in his chair. He stared at the wall for a long moment, and a look of profound, terrible understanding crossed his features. He seemed to age ten years in ten seconds.

"So," he whispered, more to himself than to them. "The French were right to be confident. And they were right to be blind. They put their faith in the Maginot Line. They put their faith in the idea that the Ardennes was impassable for tanks. They called our warnings Belgian pessimism." He gave a short, bitter laugh that held no humor. "A sickle cut. Yes. They will swing south behind the Maginot Line and cut the Allied armies in two. They will trap the British and the best of the French armies against the sea."

He slammed his fist on the desk, not in anger, but in sheer, soul crushing frustration. "And we are walking right into it! We are all walking right into it!"

He stood up and began to pace the room, his hands clasped behind his back. "Your information confirms our worst fears. Our intelligence has been reporting a buildup, but we had no idea of the scale, of the intention. The French High Command has dismissed it. They are obsessed with the attack in the north, here in Belgium. They think that is the main thrust."

He stopped and looked at the two boys, and for the first time, a glimmer of something other than despair showed in his eyes. It was a flicker of grim resolve. "You two have done the Allies a service of unimaginable importance. But it may be too late. The message must get to the French High Command and the British Expeditionary Force immediately. General Gamelin must be made to see the truth. He must shift his reserves south before the jaws of the trap close."

He strode to the door and flung it open. "Captain!" he bellowed.

The young officer appeared in an instant. "General?"

"Get me a line to General Prioux's headquarters at once! And find me the British liaison officer! Now! On the double!" The captain vanished. The general turned back to Dave and Freddy. "You will repeat your story to the British liaison. Every detail. Do not leave anything out." He paused, his eyes softening for a fraction of a second. "You are brave boys. Very brave. Your countries should be proud of you. Now, you must be hungry. And you need rest."

He was interrupted by the sudden wail of an air raid siren. It started as a low moan and rose to a piercing shriek that seemed to tear the air apart. Shouts echoed from the hallway. From far away, yet drawing closer with terrifying speed, came the high pitched, screaming whistle of falling bombs.

"Stukas!" the general swore, his face hardening. "They are hitting headquarters now. The end is coming faster than I thought."

He grabbed Dave and Freddy, one by each arm. His grip was like iron. "No time for rest! This way! To the cellars!"

He hauled them out of the office and into the crowded, frantic hallway. Officers and clerks were scrambling for the stairs. The first bomb hit with a deafening crump that shook the entire chateau to its foundations. Plaster rained down from the ceiling, and the great chandelier in the main hall swayed violently before crashing to the marble floor in a shower of crystal.

Another bomb hit closer, and the world became a nightmare of noise and concussion. The floor bucked like a wild horse, throwing them against the wall. Dave felt a searing pain in his shoulder as it slammed into the hard stone. Through the dust and chaos, he saw the general trying to shield them with his own body. The screaming of the dive bombers was directly overhead now, a sound that drilled right into your skull and turned your blood to ice.

Then came a direct hit.

Dave didn't hear the explosion so much as he felt it. It was a physical blow, a giant fist that picked him up and threw him into blackness. He was conscious of a vast, roaring noise, the feeling of falling, and a sharp, cracking impact. Then nothing.

He came to slowly, choking on dust. His head was ringing like a giant bell, and every bone in his body ached. He was lying on a pile of rubble in what seemed to be a dark, cavernous space. A single beam of dusty light lanced down from a hole somewhere above him. He tried to sit up and groaned. His left arm wouldn't move, and a sharp pain shot through his ribs.

"Freddy?" he croaked. His throat was raw. "Freddy, are you there?"

A weak moan came from a few feet away. "Dave? Is that you?"

"Yeah, it's me." Dave crawled over broken stones and splintered wood toward the sound of the voice. He found Freddy lying half buried under a pile of fallen ceiling timbers. His face was pale and streaked with blood from a cut on his forehead, but his eyes were open.

"Are you hurt?" Dave asked, his voice thick with anxiety.

"My leg," Freddy gasped. "I think it's broken. I can't move it."

Dave carefully began to pull the timbers away from his friend. They were heavy, and the effort sent waves of pain through his own injured shoulder. "What happened? Where are we?"

"The cellar, I think," Freddy said, his teeth chattering. "The chateau must have collapsed on top of us. The general... he pushed us toward the stairs just before it hit."

Dave looked around in the gloom. He could see the twisted remains of wine racks and broken barrels. They were in the cellar. Or what was left of it. He finally managed to free Freddy's leg. It was bent at an ugly angle below the knee. Just looking at it made Dave feel sick.

"What about the general?" Freddy whispered.

Dave scanned the rubble-strewn darkness. Not far away, he saw a heap of gray uniform fabric under a massive fallen beam. He crawled over to it, his heart pounding in his chest. He didn't need to look closely. The portly Belgian general who had understood the terrible truth of their message was dead. He had saved their lives at the cost of his own.

A wave of despair washed over Dave, so powerful it almost made him black out again. It was all for nothing. They had gotten the message through, but the man who understood it was gone. The headquarters was destroyed. The information was buried with them in this tomb. The sickle was still falling, and now no one was left to shout a warning.

"He's gone, Freddy," Dave said, his voice hollow. "They're all gone."

They were alone again. Wounded, trapped, and utterly, completely alone. The thunder of the war outside seemed to mock them, a celebration of the victory of chaos and destruction. Dave slumped back against a pile of bricks, the dust and the darkness closing in on him. For the first time since their ordeal began, he felt the cold, bitter sting of true hopelessness.

"It's our only chance!" Dave insisted, his eyes blazing with a wild light. "We'll never make it on the ground! We can fly low, follow the canals and rivers. We can get to the British in an hour! We have to try, Freddy! The map!"

"Alright, Dave," he said, his voice quiet. "Alright. If you think you can do it."

"I know I can," Dave said, with more confidence than he felt.

"There," the sergeant said, pointing a thick finger. "The Yser Canal. Follow it. The British are on the other side. Or they were this morning. God be with you."

Dave shook the man's hand. "Thanks. For everything." He swung himself up into the front cockpit. The controls felt strange, but blessedly familiar. He took a deep breath.

"Ready, Freddy?" he yelled over his shoulder.

"Ready as I'll ever be!" came the faint reply.

"Stand clear!" Dave shouted to the soldiers. He primed the engine and hit the ignition. The propeller coughed, sputtered, and then caught with a roar that seemed loud enough to wake the dead. The whole flimsy craft shuddered. Dave eased the throttle forward. With the Belgian soldiers pushing on the wings to get it started, the little plane lurched forward, bumping crazily across the uneven ground on its one good wheel and the wing skid.

It slewed to the left, and for a heart stopping moment Dave thought they were going to cartwheel into the river. He fought the controls, jamming the right rudder pedal to the floor. The plane straightened out. It was gathering speed. The tail came up. The bumps smoothed out as the one wheel lifted off the ground. They were flying.

He climbed just high enough to clear the treetops, then leveled out, banking to the northwest. Below them, the Belgian soldiers cheered and waved. Then they were gone, and the little plane was alone in a vast, hostile sky.

"I don't believe it," Freddy's voice came back, thin against the wind. "Dave, you're a magician!"

Dave chuckled, feeling a surge of pure elation. For the first time in days, they were not running. They were not hiding. They were masters of their own fate, soaring above the chaos. Burning farmhouses trailed plumes of black smoke into the sky. Roads were clogged with abandoned carts and military vehicles. And everywhere, there were the refugees, a pitifully long line of ants trudging endlessly westward.

Suddenly, Freddy's voice crackled with alarm. "Dave! Look! To the right!"

Dave looked. And his blood ran cold. Pouring down a side road and onto the main route was a column of German armor. Tanks, armored cars, and trucks filled with infantry, all marked with the stark black cross of the Wehrmacht. They were moving fast, unopposed. And they had seen the plane. Puffs of smoke appeared from the turrets of the armored cars as their machine guns opened up.

"Hold on!" Dave yelled. He jammed the stick forward, diving for the deck. Tracers zipped past their wings. He weaved the little plane frantically, using a line of trees for cover. He was flying so low that he could see the faces of the German soldiers as they looked up and fired at him with their rifles.

He broke clear of the column and pulled up sharply, his heart pounding. "That was close!" he gasped. "Too close!"

"They're everywhere!" Freddy shouted. "The Belgians were right! There's nothing to stop them!"

Dave gritted his teeth. He had to be more careful. He left the road and dropped down to follow the winding course of a small river, its banks providing some cover from view. They flew on for another twenty minutes, the landscape unchanging in its devastation. The elation Dave had felt was gone, replaced by a cold, gnawing anxiety. They were flying through the heart of the German advance. It was a miracle they hadn't been shot down already.

Then he saw it. Ahead of them, straight and gray, was the Yser Canal. And beyond it... beyond it was a scene of unbelievable chaos. It was the British Army. But it was not an army standing to fight. It was an army in full retreat. Thousands of trucks, guns, and tanks were streaming back from the canal, crowding every road, churning fields into mud. And beyond them, on the horizon, was the gray line of the sea, and the smoke of a burning port town.

Dunkirk.

And then the sky filled with planes. Not one or two, but dozens. They were Messerschmitts and Stukas, falling upon the retreating columns like wolves on a flock of sheep. Bombs blossomed among the trucks, and fighters strafed the roads, leaving a trail of fire and death.

"Good grief," Dave whispered in horror.

Even as he stared, a lone British Hurricane fighter tore into the German formation, its eight machine guns blazing. It sent one Stuka spiraling down in flames before two Messerschmitts pounced on it, riddling it with cannon fire. The Hurricane exploded in a ball of fire.

"Dave, they'll see us!" Freddy cried.

It was too late. A pair of Messerschmitt 109s, having finished off the Hurricane, had spotted the slow, clumsy Belgian plane. They broke off from the main dogfight and turned toward them, their shark-like noses seeming to grin with malice.

There was nowhere to run. Nowhere to hide. The little observation plane was a sitting duck.

"Hang on, Freddy!" Dave yelled, his voice tight with desperation. "I'm going down!"

He chopped the throttle and pushed the stick into a steep dive, aiming for the relative safety of the crowded roads below. He hoped they might lose them in the confusion, or that the British troops on the ground might provide some covering fire. The two German fighters followed them down, their engines screaming. The world became a blur of green fields and black smoke. The lead Messerschmitt opened fire. The bullets sounded like a drumroll on the plane's canvas skin. A line of holes appeared on the left wing. The plane shuddered violently. Dave fought to keep it level. He was a hundred feet from the ground. Fifty. The ground rushed up to meet them. He saw a field next to the road that was momentarily clear of trucks. It was their only chance. "Brace yourself!" he screamed. He pulled back on the stick at the last possible second, trying to flare for a landing. But with the damaged wing and the flat tire, the plane was unmanageable. The one good wheel touched down, the plane swerved violently, and the wingtip dug into the soft earth. The little plane cartwheeled, shedding its wings and engine in a terrible shriek of tearing metal and splintering wood, before the fuselage finally slammed to a halt, a mangled wreck in the middle of a French field.

"Where are you taking us, Captain?" the lieutenant asked.
The British officer let out a short, harsh laugh. "I have no idea where Gort's headquarters is. Nobody does. It's probably on the move right now. But I'm taking you to my brigade H.Q. He looked at Freddy, who gave him a weak but triumphant grin. They had done it. They had gotten through. Someone was listening. Here and there, the sad procession was broken by units of the Belgian army, falling back, their movements slow and disorganized. There was no fight left in them, only the instinct to survive.
"Where are they all going?" Freddy murmured, his face pressed against the dusty window.
"Away," the lieutenant said without turning around. His voice was flat, devoid of emotion. "Away from the Boche. They think the French and the British will stop them. They believe in a miracle."

The car navigated a maze of debris filled streets and finally pulled up before a large, imposing stone building that had somehow survived the bombing. Sentries in clean uniforms stood guard at the entrance, a stark contrast to the haggard soldiers they had seen in the field.
The lieutenant led them inside, through a wide corridor bustling with staff officers. Their faces were grim and tight with strain, but there was an air of frantic purpose here that had been missing at the front. They were still fighting, if only with maps and telephones.
They were led into a large office. A tall, gray haired general stood before a massive map that covered one entire wall. He was surrounded by a knot of officers who spoke in low, urgent tones. The lieutenant saluted and waited.
The general turned, his eyes tired but sharp. "What is it, Captain? I am busy."
"Sir, these boys. They have information. They have just escaped from Germany. They saw a staff map at a German command post."
The general's eyes narrowed, fixing on Dave and Freddy. For a moment, he looked as though he might dismiss them with an impatient wave. But something in their earnest, dirt smeared faces must have caught his attention.
"A map?" he said, his voice raspy. "Show me. On this map. Show me what you saw."

He pointed to the spot where they had been held, then traced the terrifying lines of advance that had been marked with black arrows and pins on the German map. He showed them the massive concentration of armor poised to strike south, to cut through the Ardennes, a move the Allied High Command had believed to be impossible.

"But, sir!" the lieutenant protested. "The roads..."

He was halfway across when the shelling started again. A shell landed in the water near the road bridge, sending a geyser of water high into the air. Then another, closer to them. The whole structure of the railway bridge shuddered from the concussion.
"Keep moving!" the lieutenant yelled from the far side.

"It's not a fairy tale!" he shouted, his voice cracking. "We saw their maps! In a German headquarters! They're swinging south of you! They're going to cut you all off from the sea!"
The captain's weary expression flickered. The word "sea" seemed to register. That was where they were all trying to go.
Dave stepped up beside Freddy. "He's telling the truth, sir," he said, his American accent cutting through the noise. "We flew out of there in a stolen plane. They shot us down just now, over there." He pointed back across the canal. "We have to warn Lord Gort."
The mention of the British Commander in Chief's name, and the quiet certainty in the American's voice, seemed to have more effect than Freddy's frantic plea. The captain stared at them, a new, calculating light in his eyes. The story was insane. But in the midst of this madness, what was one more insane story? And what if it was true?

"Yes!" Freddy said. "Pins and flags and arrows! A whole armored corps moving through the Ardennes! They're aiming for Abbeville and Boulogne!"

Dave, Freddy, and the Belgian lieutenant clambered into the cramped carrier, squeezing between soldiers who stared at them with dull curiosity.
"Where are you taking us, Captain?" the lieutenant asked.
The British officer let out a short, harsh laugh. "I have no idea where Gort's headquarters is. Nobody does. It's probably on the move right now. But I'm taking you to my brigade H.Q. It's a few miles up the road. Or it was an hour ago. My Brigadier will know what to do with you. Or he'll have you shot as spies. At this point, it's a toss up." He banged on the side of the carrier. "Get on with it, Corporal!"

He looked at Freddy, who gave him a weak but triumphant grin. They had done it. They had gotten through. Someone was listening. The tidal wave was coming, and they were standing right on the beach.

While the medic cleaned his wound with a stinging antiseptic that made him gasp, Dave listened as Freddy once again recounted their story. He looked past them, his gaze distant, as though he were already seeing the German tanks cresting the hill. "Now go. The truck is behind the building. Godspeed."

The back was already filled with wounded French soldiers, sitting silently on the floor or lying on stretchers. A corporal helped them climb in and they found a space on the floor near the tailgate.

Dave leaned his head back against the rough canvas. His arm was a solid block of pain, but it was a manageable pain now. Beside him, Freddy was quiet, his small face streaked with dirt. He looked utterly spent. The truck lurched into motion, bouncing onto the broken road. Through a gap in the canvas, Dave could see the ruined village of Briel sliding away behind them. He saw the French captain standing in the street, watching them go, a lonely, defiant figure amid the destruction.

The truck picked up speed, heading west. West toward Arras. West, away from the advancing German tide. For the first time in what felt like an eternity, they were moving with the current, not against it. But Dave felt no joy, no triumph. The captain's words echoed in his head. Pray that it is not already too late. He looked at the silent, wounded men around him, listened to the ceaseless thunder of the guns behind them, and a cold certainty settled in his heart. Their escape was over. But the war, the real war, had only just begun.

We are ordered to retreat to a new line just outside of a village called Briel. It is three kilometers from here. I have a motorcycle. It is not much, but it is fast. I can take one of you with me."

Dave's heart sank. One of them. He looked at Freddy. The kid was exhausted, but he was unhurt. Dave, on the other hand, was wounded and fading fast. The choice was obvious.

"Take Freddy," Dave said, his voice raspy. "Get him to the Allied lines. He can tell them what we saw. The map. He knows it all."

Freddy's head snapped up. "No! I'm not leaving you, Dave! Absolutely not!"

"Don't be a fool, Freddy," Dave said, trying to put some force into his words. "One of us has to get through. You're in better shape. You have to go."

"No!" Freddy insisted, his chin jutting out. "We started this together, and we'll finish it together! I'm not leaving you here to be captured!"

The Lieutenant watched them both, a strange expression on his tired face. "He is right," he said quietly. "The Boche will be through these woods in less than an hour. If you stay here, you will be a prisoner again. Or worse." He looked from one to the other. "You are good friends. It is a rare thing in these times." He made a sudden decision. "All right. We will all go. Both of you on the motorcycle with me. It will be slow. It will be a heavy load. But we will try."

Hope, fragile and unexpected, fluttered in Dave's chest. "You'd do that?"

"I am a soldier," the Lieutenant said simply. "My job is to fight the enemy. Getting your information to G.H.Q. is part of that fight. Now, no more talking." He helped Dave to his feet, supporting him with a surprisingly strong arm. "Come. My men are already pulling out. We must be quick."

He led them deeper into the woods, following a narrow, winding path. All around them, the Belgian soldiers were retreating. They moved quietly, without panic, their faces set in grim, determined lines. They were beaten, but they were not broken. They carried their rifles and their machine guns and their wounded, their boots making soft sounds on the damp earth. It was the picture of an army in retreat, an army that had been battered and smashed but refused to shatter.

They came to a small clearing where a motorcycle with a sidecar was hidden under a camouflage net. It was a heavy, powerful looking machine. "Here," the Lieutenant said. "You," he pointed to Dave, "get in the sidecar. It will be a rough ride, but you must hold on. And you," he looked at Freddy, "you will ride behind me. Hold on to my belt and do not let go, no matter what happens. Understood?"

They both nodded. Freddy helped ease Dave into the cramped sidecar. Every jolt sent a fresh wave of fire up Dave's arm. He gritted his teeth, the world swimming in and out of focus. Freddy climbed onto the seat behind the Lieutenant and wrapped his arms tightly around the man's waist.

The Lieutenant kicked the starter. The engine roared to life with a deafening cough, then settled into a throbbing growl. "Here we go," he shouted over the noise. "To Briel! And may God be with us!"

He let out the clutch and the motorcycle leaped forward, bumping and bouncing over the forest floor. Dave clung to the side of the car, his knuckles white. Trees whipped past them. They burst out of the woods onto a narrow dirt road. The Lieutenant didn't slow down. He twisted the throttle and the bike shot forward, engine screaming.

The road was a nightmare. It was choked with refugees, a slow moving river of human misery. Old men pushing wheelbarrows piled high with possessions. Women carrying babies. Frightened children with wide, staring eyes. They were all trudging west, away from the guns. The Lieutenant weaved the motorcycle through them, shouting warnings in French, his hand constantly on the horn.

Dave's head lolled against the side of the car. The faces of the refugees blurred past him. They were blank, stunned, exhausted. It was the face of a whole country that had been struck a mortal blow. He saw the tidal wave again in his mind, but this time it was not just an idea. It was here. It was this road. This flood of broken people was what the wave left in its wake.

A new sound joined the chorus of the engine and the distant guns. A high pitched whine. Dave knew it instantly. Planes. He forced his head up and scanned the sky. There they were. Three black specks, circling high above. Messerschmitts.

"Boche fighters!" Freddy yelled in the Lieutenant's ear.

The Lieutenant had seen them too. He twisted the throttle even further, urging every last ounce of speed from the laboring engine. The road ahead was clear for a hundred yards. "Hold on!" he roared.

There was nowhere to hide. They were a perfect target on the open road. Dave watched, mesmerized with a sort of fatalistic calm, as one of the specks peeled off from the others and began to dive. It grew larger and larger, its wings sharp and black against the gray sky.

The refugees on the road saw it too. A wave of panic spread through the crowd. People screamed and scattered, diving for the ditches on either side of the road. A cart overturned, spilling furniture and clothing everywhere.

The Messerschmitt was coming in low, its guns winking. The Lieutenant swerved the motorcycle violently to the left, then to the right, making them a difficult target. Tracer rounds stitched a line in the dirt just behind them. The plane screamed overhead, its engine noise a physical blow.

"He's coming around again!" Freddy shouted.

Dave saw the second fighter start its dive. This was it. They couldn't be this lucky twice. He closed his eyes, waiting for the impact. But instead of the roar of machine guns, he heard a new sound. A sharp, angry rattling from somewhere nearby. He opened his eyes. On a small hill just off the road, a Belgian machine gun crew, part of the retreating rear guard, had set up their weapon. They were firing at the diving Messerschmitt, their tracers reaching up like fiery fingers.

The German pilot clearly hadn't expected resistance. He broke off his attack and pulled up sharply. The machine gun crew kept firing, hounding him as he climbed. His wingman, seeing his partner driven off, gave up the attack as well. The two fighters joined their leader and flew off to the east, looking for easier prey.

The Lieutenant slowed the motorcycle and raised a hand in salute to the gunners on the hill. One of them, a burly man with a thick mustache, waved back. Then the Lieutenant gunned the engine again and they sped onward.

"Boy," Dave breathed, his body trembling with the aftershock of adrenaline. "Those guys saved our skins."

"Belgian soldiers do not run," the Lieutenant said, his voice tight with pride. "We may retreat. But we do not run."

They reached the outskirts of Briel a few minutes later. It was what was left of a village. Most of the houses were rubble. The church steeple had been blown clean off. French soldiers were everywhere, digging in, setting up anti tank guns, turning the ruined village into a fortress. They had the same exhausted, grimy look as the Belgians, but there were more of them, and their equipment looked newer, heavier.

The Lieutenant brought the motorcycle to a halt beside a makeshift command post set up in the cellar of a destroyed bakery. A French captain with a bloodstained bandage around his head looked up as they approached.

"My friend," the Lieutenant said to the captain in French, "I have brought you a gift. Two pilots, one English, one American. They have important information for your High Command. And this one," he gestured to Dave, "needs a doctor. Badly."

The French captain stared at them with weary, intelligent eyes. "Pilots? Where is your plane?"

"In a crater about twenty kilometers that way," Freddy piped up, also in French. "We have just come from Germany. We have seen their invasion plans."

The captain's eyebrows shot up. He looked from Freddy's earnest face to Dave's pale, sweating one. He barked an order to a nearby soldier. "Get the medic! At once!" Then he looked back at them. "Come. Down here. Tell me everything."

He helped the Lieutenant get Dave out of the sidecar and half carried him down the stone steps into the cellar. The air was cool and smelled of damp earth and stale bread. A medic, a young man with a thin mustache, was already there. He immediately set to work on Dave's arm, cutting away the bloody sleeve.

"Now," the captain said, pulling a map out and spreading it on an ammunition crate. "Show me."

While the medic cleaned his wound with a stinging antiseptic that made him gasp, Dave listened as Freddy once again recounted their story. He spoke quickly and clearly, his finger tracing lines on the French captain's map, pointing out the locations of the German armored spearheads he had memorized.

The captain listened in grim silence, his expression growing darker with every word. When Freddy finished, the officer stared at the map for a long time. The medic was bandaging Dave's arm now, a tight, professional job. The pain was already subsiding into a dull throb.

Finally, the captain looked up. "Sacre bleu," he whispered. "It is worse than we thought. They are moving faster. They are aiming here." He jabbed a finger at a spot on the map far to the west of them. "They mean to cut us off completely. To push the British right into the sea." He folded the map with a snap. "This information must get to General Blanchard at once."

He looked at the Belgian Lieutenant. "Thank you, my friend. You have done a great service to France today."

Lieutenant Dubois simply nodded. "I must return to my men. We are forming a new line with your troops on the canal." He looked at Dave and Freddy. "Good luck, my brave little ones." He gave them a tired smile, saluted the captain, and was gone.

"And you two," the captain said, turning his attention back to them. "You are heroes." He saw them flush and shook his head. "No, it is true. But your journey is not over." He pointed to the cellar entrance. "I have a dispatch truck leaving for Arras in ten minutes. It will carry wounded. You will go with it. It is the best I can do."

"Thank you, Captain," Dave said, feeling a wave of relief so powerful it almost made him dizzy. Arras. They were actually going to make it.

"Do not thank me," the captain said, his face hardening. "Just pray the truck gets through. The roads are a shooting gallery. And pray that your information is not already too late." He looked past them, his gaze distant, as though he were already seeing the German tanks cresting the hill. "Now go. The truck is behind the building. Godspeed."

They climbed the steps back into the gray, smoky daylight. A large canvas covered truck was waiting, its engine idling. The back was already filled with wounded French soldiers, sitting silently on the floor or lying on stretchers. A corporal helped them climb in and they found a space on the floor near the tailgate.

Dave leaned his head back against the rough canvas. His arm was a solid block of pain, but it was a manageable pain now. Beside him, Freddy was quiet, his small face streaked with dirt. He looked utterly spent. The truck lurched into motion, bouncing onto the broken road. Through a gap in the canvas, Dave could see the ruined village of Briel sliding away behind them. He saw the French captain standing in the street, watching them go, a lonely, defiant figure amid the destruction.

The truck picked up speed, heading west. West toward Arras. West, away from the advancing German tide. For the first time in what felt like an eternity, they were moving with the current, not against it. But Dave felt no joy, no triumph. The captain's words echoed in his head. Pray that it is not already too late. He looked at the silent, wounded men around him, listened to the ceaseless thunder of the guns behind them, and a cold certainty settled in his heart. Their escape was over. But the war, the real war, had only just begun.
